questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/5907cf8a9103cc9a639fd8078da3646cc0395d28827f58c0f1beef0a1c06645b.png)

The triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over the region $R$ (shown above) can be expressed as the following repeated integral:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$

Rewrite this repeated integral by integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ and then $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the given repeated integral, we see that $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le y,\,\,0\le z\le {y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}
$$

We wish to rewrite our triple integral as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/a89646433c8851f66c94092b75fae7b46b01f31c69ca03d338464b87bd7f5df4.png)

The region $D$ is a type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le y}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the bottom boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is 

$$
x=y\,⟹\,y=x
$$

and the top boundary of the region is

$$
y=1.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region $D$ is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,x\le y\le 1},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/1604e44050208cfb3b4dd81d35bff9769c7498d8304583d5ba92ad4b2f62fd05.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem:
By changing the order of integration, find the missing limits in the following repeated integral.

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}-2}^{y}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y={\int }_{-3}^{p}{\int }_{-1}^{q}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{r}^{1}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{{v}_{3}(y)}^{{v}_{4}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{3}(x,y)}^{{u}_{4}(x,y)}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt[3]{y}-2\le x\le y,\,\,\frac{y}{2}\le z\le x+4}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}-2}^{y}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{{v}_{3}(x)}^{{v}_{4}(x)}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/c92ab09dc71043ac3f5265202f36e38110e5e8db9f2dd115ab006721ed66d4c0.png)

The region $D$ is a type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,\sqrt[3]{y}-2\le x\le y}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we split $D$ into two type I regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/8ac0e7631d0baa8ba3b4c37ebe2b2b1d8efa650495d197f425aba093f342a9d3.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=-1\,$ and $\,y=(x+2)^{3}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=x\,$ and $\,y=1.$

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-3\le x\le -1,\,-1\le y\le (x+2)^{3}}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,x\le y\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{-1}{\int }_{-1}^{(x+2)^{3}}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{\int }_{y/2}^{x+4}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region $D$ is

$$

$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

$$

$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(x),$ is

$$
x=\sqrt{z}\,⟹\,z={x}^{2}
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
z=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/7e684766b85a214d1f1dd7845979052c532e11ecce74d0284b8fc379b5669957.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{e}^{z/x}]_{z=0}^{z={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x{e}^{x}-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[(x-1){e}^{x}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-\frac{1}{2})-(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z)/2}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{2yz}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le x\le 2yz}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{0}^{2yz}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/d3865f790df8c2a228f08c290a113954687ade63a275a754c4cb3199c234d5ec.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
z=0
$$

and the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(y),$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z\,⟹\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡2y.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,0\le z\le \operatorname{sin}⁡2y},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/085b2ce5a9ecd2632f70f287bbef5e9f04566871fc8adf7ba10076e2e875ca2e.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z)/2}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{2yz}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}{\int }_{0}^{2yz}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}[{\int }_{0}^{2yz}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{z})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}{[-z\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{z})]}_{x=0}^{x=2yz}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}(-z\operatorname{cos}⁡2y+z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}z(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2y)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2y){\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}z\,\text{d}z]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2y){[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2y){sin}^{2}⁡2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡2y\,\text{d}y-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2y\,{sin}^{2}⁡2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4y)\,\text{d}y-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2y\,{sin}^{2}⁡2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[y-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4y]}_{0}^{\pi /4}-\frac{1}{12}[{sin}^{3}⁡2y]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0)-\frac{1}{12}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -4}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
By changing the order of integration in the following repeated integrals so that they are integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ and then $x,$ express the following sum as a single repeated integral.

$$
\displaystyle
\int_{-1}^0 \int_{y^2}^{1} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y
+
\int_0^1 \int_{y}^{1} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)}  f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integrals, we see that the domain of integration $R = R_1\cup R_2,$ where $R_1$ and $R_2$ are type I regions, is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{1} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}}, \\ {R}_{2} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

$$
D =
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq y \leq 0, \quad y^2 \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
\:\cup\:
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the lower boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=y^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y = -\sqrt{x}
$$

and the upper boundary of the region is

$$
x=y
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y =x.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad -\sqrt{x} \leq y \leq  x \right\},

canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate
$\displaystyle
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{y}^{1} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.$

*Hint: Change change the order of integration to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: y \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq y \right\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/bdd856ef8a7940a009b7ee27d6614fdb8c042e6655c2316ce4db0633bfd04e9f.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $y = y(x),$ is

$$
x = y \qquad\Longrightarrow \qquad y = x
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y = 0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq x \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/1e28e1cef9743da80d6fd2d38840810b12239d8546254c4d4cca767568f76a53.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[z]_{0}^{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3y{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{{x}^{3}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$
